name: Paternalistic conservatism
scope: The strand of conservatism in which those with authority, wealth or privilege take moral responsibility for protecting the poorer and weaker, in order to keep order, social cohesion and existing institutions, and to head off Marxist revolution (Gjorshoski 2016, 'Paternalistic conservatism'). Its sources give Burke as an early writer, Disraeli's Toryism as its 'purest form' and Bismarck's 1880s compulsory insurance laws as the continental case, and add the later Anglo-Saxon and Western European conservative parties' social protection, Keynesian full-employment policy, corporatist partnership in firms and agricultural support. The source calls its motive 'more pragmatic than idealistic'. Excludes the neoliberal, neoconservative and Christian-democratic variants the same source treats separately, and one-nation conservatism, Red Toryism, Tory democracy or other ideologies' sources, which are not used here.

notes: Phase 1 (scope). Only one defining source naming the ideology was found open: Gjorshoski 2016. The SEP 'Conservatism' entry, EBSCO and tutor2u pages saved in the source folder discuss one-nation conservatism or conservatism and never name paternalistic conservatism, so are not cited. Andrew Heywood's Political Ideologies (2007, 2012), Vincent 2009 and Dorey 1995, which Wikipedia cites, are lending-only. The two downloaded books are not used: Heywood, Samuel, High church politics (1792) is a different author from Andrew Heywood and is about test-act disputes; Steinberg, Bismarck: A Life never uses the name or 'paternalistic' (checked by grep), so it is a biography of one person, a coatrack for the ideology. Key figures: Disraeli (a key figure of one-nation-conservatism) and Burke (of conservatism) are named by the source but belong to those ideologies, so none is listed. Answers: only Gjorshoski (s5) defines the ideology under its name, so answers rest on it alone and most statements are null. Themes searched in it: welfare and social insurance, class relations, nation and patriotism, corporatism and firms, agriculture, state and revolution, pragmatism, hierarchy. The earlier pass's answers rested on Wikipedia (s1, s4), the SEP entry on conservatism (s2) and Disraeli's speech (s3), none of which are a defining source naming the ideology; they are changed or nulled with the old versions kept in each answer's history. summary: Paternalistic conservatism, as Gjorshoski describes it, holds that those with authority and means have a moral responsibility to protect the weaker and poorer, from motives that are more pragmatic than idealistic: keeping order, social cohesion and existing institutions and heading off Marxist revolution. In practice it means social protection for workers (Bismarck's compulsory insurance), a unified nation held together by welfare and patriotism, partnership between classes and corporatist cooperation in firms, and care for agriculture, while keeping a market economy and a moderate hierarchy.
